_readme: REWARD LEVER INVENTORY — DAVID OWNS THIS FILE (R8; same doctrine as signal_lenses.json). The named mechanisms that exist in UK reward practice, surfaced in an Options block beside a gap — NEVER ranked, scored, starred or ordered by fit (file order only; an ordered list is an implied recommendation). Every lever carries a trade_off — a lever with no stated downside is marketing. No vendor, provider or product is ever named. register_effect says which register the lever moves: 'Substance' (position/provision — what you offer or how much) or 'Approach' (practice — how you operate); a member behind on POSITION needs a Substance lever, one CONTRADICTED on practice needs an Approach lever. typical_shape is domain knowledge unless prevalence_metric_id links a measured metric (then peer take-up renders live). v1 tranche per R8: Pay, Benefits & Lifestyle, Time Off & Family (the three densest evidence categories); Governance is the ruled second tranche. TRANCHE 2 (2026-08-16): extended from three categories to ALL EIGHT so no domain section in the reward report ends on 'a later tranche' where the reader expects recommendations. Every category now carries BOTH registers (Substance for a position gap, Approach for a coherence contradiction), so no gap can land without options. The 20 new levers are CLAUDE-DRAFTED and need David's review the same way the first 12 did. STATUS: drafted 2026-08-14 — pending David's content sign-off; refine, reject or extend freely. REPAIR 2026-08-16: PEN-CONTRIBUTION carried prevalence_metric_id 'REW26_BEN_PENS_EMPLOYER', which does not exist in the question bank — the link resolved to nothing and the lever rendered with no peer take-up, silently. The key is REMOVED rather than repointed: every other prevalence link reads a yes_no or single_select ('what share of peers do this'), and an employer contribution RATE is a matrix benchmark, not a prevalence. If you want a link here, the candidates are REW26_BEN_PENSION_MATCH (matching offered) or REW264_PEN_CONTRIBTIER (contributions rise with service/level) — both are practices, not rates. See R7_R8_RULING_SHEET_2026-08-16.md. REPAIR 2026-08-16 (practitioner panel): BEN-SALSAC described pre-2017 salary-sacrifice law (cars/technology NI advantage removed by the OpRA rules) — five of five reviewers flagged it; INC-RECOGNITION was mis-costed one-off (voucher spend is recurring and taxable); BEN-GRISK claimed claims-experience re-rating, wrong for a unit-rated scheme at this size; PEN-CONTRIBUTION was mis-anchored to the AE minimum and overstated candidate visibility and lock-in; GOV-RANGES-INTERNAL recast one-off for its correction cases. Factual repairs only — David's R8 sign-off still owed on all wording.

levers.name: Formal pay bands with published progression
levers.what_it_is: Defined salary ranges per grade, with the rules for moving through them written down.
levers.typical_shape: Bands built from survey data around a target market position, refreshed annually; progression tied to a documented mechanism.
levers.trade_off: Bands surface every existing anomaly the day they are shared — budget for correction cases before, not after.

levers.name: Merit matrix for the annual review
levers.what_it_is: Pay increases set by the combination of performance rating and position in range.
levers.typical_shape: A published grid; higher increases for strong performers low in range, tapering at range maximum.
levers.trade_off: Only as credible as the performance ratings feeding it — rating inflation quietly flattens the differentiation it promises.

levers.name: Pay-for-skills premiums
levers.what_it_is: Defined premiums for named scarce skills or certifications, separate from the base structure.
levers.typical_shape: A short list of premium-bearing skills reviewed each year; premiums lapse when scarcity does.
levers.trade_off: Premiums are easy to grant and politically hard to remove once the scarcity passes.

levers.name: Targeted adjustment pot
levers.what_it_is: A ring-fenced slice of the review budget for correcting specific market or equity gaps rather than spreading it evenly.
levers.typical_shape: A minority share of the annual budget held back and allocated case-by-case against benchmark evidence.
levers.trade_off: Everyone not in the pot gets a smaller flat award that year — the fairness story has to be told, not assumed.

levers.name: Flexible benefits allowance
levers.what_it_is: A per-employee allowance spent across a menu of benefits instead of one fixed package.
levers.typical_shape: A core of protected benefits plus a flexible allowance; enrolment windows once or twice a year.
levers.trade_off: Platform and administration costs are real and permanent; take-up disappoints where communication is thin.

levers.name: Salary-sacrifice arrangements
levers.what_it_is: Benefits funded from gross pay where the tax rules still allow it — pension, cycle-to-work, ultra-low-emission cars — with automatic-enrolment compliance preserved and pay never sacrificed below the wage floor.
levers.typical_shape: Pension by default, with car and technology schemes added where the workforce profile suits.
levers.trade_off: Since the 2017 rules most other benefits lost the advantage, and the employer chooses whether to share its NI saving; announced NIC changes may cap the pension saving in future.

levers.name: Group risk bundle
levers.what_it_is: Life assurance, income protection and critical illness bought together as an insured bundle.
levers.typical_shape: Life cover for all staff with income protection layered on for salaried populations.
levers.trade_off: At this workforce size schemes are typically unit-rated, so premiums move with workforce age, profile and market rates at each review — the cost is not fixed at purchase.

levers.name: Voluntary benefits platform
levers.what_it_is: Employee-paid benefits at group rates — discounts, insurance top-ups, financial products — at low employer cost.
levers.typical_shape: A discounts core with optional employee-funded insurances alongside.
levers.trade_off: Perceived value is far below paid benefits — it widens choice, it does not read as investment.

levers.name: Enhanced family leave
levers.what_it_is: Maternity, paternity and adoption pay above the statutory floor.
levers.typical_shape: A stepped enhancement — a period at full pay, then a period at half pay, service-gated.
levers.trade_off: Effectively irreversible — withdrawing family pay reads as bad faith, so the commitment is permanent from day one.

levers.name: Holiday purchase / sale
levers.what_it_is: Employees buy or sell a capped number of leave days through payroll.
levers.typical_shape: Up to a week each way, elected once a year alongside benefits enrolment.
levers.trade_off: Payroll and accrual administration is fiddly, and heavy selling can quietly signal an overwork problem.

levers.name: Occupational sick pay above SSP
levers.what_it_is: Company sick pay for a defined period before statutory rates apply.
levers.typical_shape: Service-banded full-pay then half-pay periods, with absence triggers managed alongside.
levers.trade_off: Costs concentrate in the highest-absence populations, and tightening a scheme later is far harder than never enhancing it.

levers.name: Paid carer's leave
levers.what_it_is: Paid time off for caring responsibilities beyond the statutory unpaid entitlement.
levers.typical_shape: A small number of paid days a year, claimed without evidence requirements.
levers.trade_off: Low headline cost but hard to forecast — usage is invisible until the policy exists.

levers.name: A defined annual bonus plan
levers.what_it_is: A written variable-pay plan with a named population, a target percentage and the measures it pays against.
levers.typical_shape: Target percentages set by level, funded from a pool tied to company performance, with individual outcomes moderated at a calibration meeting.
levers.trade_off: Once a target percentage is published people plan around it, so a lean year reads as a cut rather than a variable outcome.

levers.name: A non-cash recognition scheme
levers.what_it_is: A structured way for colleagues and managers to mark good work, usually with vouchers, points or awards rather than salary.
levers.typical_shape: A small per-award value with a budget per manager, plus an annual awards moment; spend is visible and capped.
levers.trade_off: An annual award budget, not a one-off: voucher and points awards are taxable earnings unless each sits within the trivial-benefits exemption, so the real cost includes the tax treatment.

levers.name: Performance differentiation in the pay review
levers.what_it_is: A stated mechanism that gives different increases to different performance outcomes, rather than one rate for everyone.
levers.typical_shape: A matrix pairing performance outcome with position in range, published to managers with a worked example.
levers.trade_off: Differentiation only reads as fair where performance outcomes themselves are trusted; introduced onto a weak review process it transfers the argument to pay.

levers.name: Written incentive governance
levers.what_it_is: The rules of the plan set down: who is eligible, how outcomes are decided, what happens to leavers and on a change of role.
levers.typical_shape: A short plan document approved once a year, with the discretion points named rather than implied.
levers.trade_off: Writing the discretion down removes the room to make exceptions quietly, which is sometimes the point and sometimes the loss.

levers.name: A higher employer contribution
levers.what_it_is: Raising what the employer puts in beyond its current rate towards the market's, either across the board or at defined levels.
levers.typical_shape: A flat uplift of one or two percentage points, or a new top band for longer-service or senior populations.
levers.trade_off: Pension spend is rarely weighed by candidates at offer stage, and reducing employer contributions later means consultation and a real goodwill cost — it buys retention far better than attraction.

levers.name: A matching structure
levers.what_it_is: Employer contributions that rise with what the employee chooses to put in, up to a stated ceiling.
levers.typical_shape: Match to a cap of a few percent, with the ceiling published alongside the default.
levers.trade_off: Matching rewards those who can afford to save, so it widens the gap between higher and lower earners unless the default is set generously.

levers.name: Salary sacrifice as the default
levers.what_it_is: Running pension contributions through sacrifice by default rather than on request, with an opt-out.
levers.typical_shape: Default enrolment into sacrifice at the existing contribution level; the National Insurance saving is either kept or shared.
levers.trade_off: Sacrifice reduces the pay figure used for some borrowing and state calculations, so it needs explaining to lower earners rather than defaulting silently.

levers.name: Financial wellbeing support
levers.what_it_is: Guidance, tools or workplace saving that help people manage money now, alongside the pension that pays later.
levers.typical_shape: Sessions at key moments, a modelling tool, and sometimes a payroll-linked savings or loan facility.
levers.trade_off: Support is judged on whether it changes anything; offered without follow-through it reads as a gesture.

levers.name: Private medical cover
levers.what_it_is: Employer-funded medical insurance, usually with a defined population and an option to add family at cost.
levers.typical_shape: Core cover for all employees or a senior population, with employee-paid family upgrades.
levers.trade_off: Premiums rise with claims and with the age of the population, so this is the benefit most likely to cost more next year than it does this year.

levers.name: A health cash plan
levers.what_it_is: Cover that reimburses everyday health costs — dental, optical, physiotherapy — rather than major treatment.
levers.typical_shape: A low per-head monthly premium across the whole workforce, with claim limits by category.
levers.trade_off: It is used and valued far more widely than medical insurance, but it does not answer the waiting-list question that medical cover is bought for.

levers.name: Group income protection
levers.what_it_is: Insured replacement income if someone is unable to work for an extended period, usually with rehabilitation support attached.
levers.typical_shape: A percentage of salary after a deferred period, often with the insurer's return-to-work service included.
levers.trade_off: The rehabilitation service is often the part that pays for itself, and the part nobody remembers is included.

levers.name: Levelling who is eligible
levers.what_it_is: Extending existing protection cover to populations currently excluded, rather than buying new cover.
levers.typical_shape: Removing grade or hours thresholds so part-time and frontline colleagues hold the same core cover.
levers.trade_off: Levelling up is visible and welcome; it also sets a floor that is very hard to lower again if costs move.

levers.name: An employee assistance programme
levers.what_it_is: A confidential support line and short-course counselling, available to employees and usually their households.
levers.typical_shape: A per-head annual fee with unlimited access to the line and a set number of sessions per issue.
levers.trade_off: Take-up is low everywhere unless it is promoted repeatedly, so the cost is small and the visible return is slow.

levers.name: Named mental health support
levers.what_it_is: Trained first-contact colleagues, manager guidance, and a route to clinical help that people can find without asking a manager.
levers.typical_shape: A trained cohort across sites, refreshed annually, with a published route to the clinical pathway.
levers.trade_off: Trained colleagues carry real weight for others; without supervision and a clear boundary the support becomes a burden they did not sign up for.

levers.name: A stated wellbeing framework
levers.what_it_is: Setting out what the organisation covers and what it does not, so provision reads as a position rather than a collection.
levers.typical_shape: Three or four named strands with the provision under each, reviewed annually against use.
levers.trade_off: A framework makes the gaps as visible as the provision, which is useful internally and uncomfortable in a year with no budget to fill them.

levers.name: Manager capability on wellbeing
levers.what_it_is: Equipping managers to hold the early conversation and to know where it goes next.
levers.typical_shape: Short practical training tied to the absence and return-to-work process, rather than a standalone course.
levers.trade_off: This is the lever with the widest reach and the least visible output — it shows up in absence and turnover long before anyone credits it.

levers.name: Publishing pay ranges internally
levers.what_it_is: Making the range for a role visible to the people in it, with the rules for moving through it.
levers.typical_shape: Range and progression rules visible on the intranet or in the HR system, released alongside a manager briefing.
levers.trade_off: Publishing ranges surfaces every anomaly at once — the correction budget and the manager script both need to exist before the release, not after.

levers.name: Pay ranges in job adverts
levers.what_it_is: Stating the range on the advert rather than at offer stage.
levers.typical_shape: The full range or the first two thirds of it, applied consistently across levels.
levers.trade_off: Candidates self-select on the number before they hear anything else, which shortens hiring and loses some people who would have been persuadable.

levers.name: A fixed pay review cycle
levers.what_it_is: A published annual timetable for how pay is reviewed, decided and communicated.
levers.typical_shape: A dated cycle with the moderation step and the communication window named in it.
levers.trade_off: A fixed cycle ends ad-hoc rises, which is the point and also the thing managers will miss most in the first year.

levers.name: Total reward statements
levers.what_it_is: Showing each person the full value of what they receive, not just the salary line.
levers.typical_shape: An annual per-person statement covering pay, pension, insured benefits and time off.
levers.trade_off: Statements raise the perceived value of what already exists, and they also show clearly where a package is thin.

levers.name: A stated benefits position
levers.what_it_is: Setting out what the package is meant to lead on, so provision reads as a choice rather than an accumulation.
levers.typical_shape: Two or three named priorities with the provision under each, reviewed annually against take-up.
levers.trade_off: Naming what the package leads on also names what it does not, which is a harder conversation in a year with no budget.

levers.name: Benefits communication and take-up
levers.what_it_is: Making existing provision visible and easy to use, rather than buying more of it.
levers.typical_shape: A refreshed benefits page, moments-that-matter prompts, and take-up reported back annually.
levers.trade_off: Communication raises the perceived value of what exists and does nothing for a benefit that is genuinely missing — it cannot substitute for provision.

levers.name: Written leave policies with worked examples
levers.what_it_is: Setting out entitlement, pay and the request route for each type of leave, in language people can act on.
levers.typical_shape: One page per leave type with a worked example, and the manager decision points named.
levers.trade_off: Clear policies raise take-up of leave people were already entitled to, which is the intent and also a real cover cost.

levers.name: Consistent entitlement across populations
levers.what_it_is: Removing differences in leave entitlement between groups that are not deliberate.
levers.typical_shape: An audit of entitlement by contract type and site, levelling to a single stated position.
levers.trade_off: Levelling up is welcomed and hard to undo; levelling down needs consultation and rarely saves what it costs in goodwill.
